query: Single-phase ZrB2 benefits from strong Zr–B and B–B interactions and a high melting point, but it requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and does not readily meet application requirements on its own. Earlier studies sought to lower the required temperature, yet the resulting materials remained vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation or liquid plating-metal corrosion, while reported preparation temperatures generally remained above 1700 °C. Under the constraints of lower-temperature manufacture, adequate strength and structural integrity, oxidation durability, and prolonged service in a liquid plating bath, what single intervention could overcome these limitations? Provide one hypothesis specifying the intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome compared with single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens, applicable preparation and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment evaluating final body quality, structural integrity, oxidation, and liquid-metal corrosion that would falsify the hypothesis if its predictions were not observed.

generation.hypothesis: Applying oscillatory pressure sintering to single‐phase ZrB2 at lower processing temperatures (<1700 °C) will refine the microstructure (by promoting enhanced densification and grain boundary bonding) and thereby yield a material with improved mechanical strength, oxidation resistance, and liquid metal corrosion durability compared with both conventionally high‐temperature sintered ZrB2 and prior lower‐temperature specimens.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase ZrB2 powder precursors or green compacts prepared in a standard way for sintering
generation.intervention: Employ oscillatory pressure sintering (e.g., using cyclic mechanical loading at around 9 Hz) during densification at temperatures below 1700 °C
generation.conditions: Sintering performed at temperatures significantly lower than 2300 °C (targeting <1700 °C) with controlled oscillatory pressure; subsequent testing at high-temperature oxidation conditions (e.g., 1300 °C) and in simulated liquid plating-metal baths
generation.structural_mediator: Grain refinement and improved inter-particle bonding that reduce porosity and promote a more continuous, protective oxide formation at high temperature
generation.mechanism: The oscillatory pressure facilitates enhanced diffusion and consolidation at lower temperatures by periodically perturbing the forming microstructure. This leads to a denser material with finer grains. The refined grain structure can promote the formation of more uniformly protective surface oxides during high-temperature exposure and resist penetration by liquid plating metals, simultaneously increasing hardness and structural integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The oscillatory pressure sintered ZrB2 should exhibit mechanical properties (e.g., hardness and fracture toughness) at least comparable to traditional high-temperature (≥2300 °C) sintered samples, while significantly slowing oxidation-induced mass loss (targeting reductions similar in scale to an ~80% improvement seen in related systems) and improved stability in liquid metal plating environments compared to lower-temperature specimens sintered without pressure oscillation.
generation.baseline: Properties of conventional single-phase ZrB2 specimens sintered at high temperature (>2300 °C) and those prepared at lower temperatures (~1700 °C) without oscillatory pressure
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is limited to processing at sintering temperatures below 1700 °C, oxidation exposure near 1300 °C, and liquid metal plating conditions that mimic typical service environments; extrapolation outside these conditions remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty over the direct transfer of improvements observed in doped Mo-Si-B alloy systems using oscillatory sintering to pure ZrB2, particularly in fully replicating the desired balance of oxidation resistance and liquid metal durability. The quantitative extent of mechanical and chemical improvements in single-phase ZrB2 needs experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of single-phase ZrB2 samples: one using conventional pressure-less or static pressure sintering at temperatures above 2300 °C and the other utilizing oscillatory pressure sintering under sub-1700 °C conditions. Characterize the microstructure (grain size, density) via SEM/TEM. Assess mechanical properties (hardness, fracture toughness) using standardized tests. Conduct high-temperature oxidation tests at 1300 °C to measure mass loss and expose samples to a simulated liquid plating-metal bath to evaluate corrosion resistance.
measurements: Grain size distribution and density (SEM/TEM, Archimedes method)
Thermogravimetric measurements of mass loss during oxidation
Corrosion rate and surface integrity after liquid metal exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If oscillatory pressure sintered ZrB2 samples do not show statistically significant improvements in microstructural refinement, mechanical properties, a reduction in oxidation-induced mass loss (ideally approaching an ~80% improvement), and enhanced resistance to liquid metal corrosion compared with both traditional high-temperature sintered and lower-temperature non-oscillatory specimens, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractOscillatory pressure sintering is a novel crystal refinement technology. The doping of different concentrations of ZrB2 under oscillatory sintering technology (9 Hz) is discussed here, focusing on its macroscopic mechanics and oxidation resistance. In particular, doping 2.5 wt% ZrB2 can effectively increase the hardness of the alloy, slightly increase the fracture toughness of the alloy and have an outstanding effect on the oxidation resistance of the alloy at 1300 °C, achieving the effect of reducing mass loss by 80.3%.Keywords: oscillatory sintering, Mo-9Si-8B alloy, ZrB2 addition
## 1. Introduction
The excellent high-temperature properties of Mo-Si-B alloys have attracted much attention in the past three decades, and they have a great prospect in replacing nickel-based alloys and the static rings of high-pressure turbine guide [,,]. Molybdenum is a typical refractory metal with a high melting point of about 2870 K, but its oxidation resistance is poor, so it is difficult to use it as a high-temperature structural material alone [].
